feed.desc: Investors Matter for the Future of Trustworthy AI. Are they ready?    OECD AI Policy Observatory
summaryLinesEn: Investors see AI trustworthiness as financially material At the GPAI Expert Group on Trustworthy AI Investment meeting, held on 11 June 2026, one message emerged clearly from discussions across public and private markets: investors no longer view trustworthy AI as a purely ethical consideration.

The GPAI Expert Group on Trustworthy AI Investment wants to help bridge this gap by examining how investors can help advance trustworthy AI by integrating governance, accountability and risk management considerations into investment decisions.

But when investment committees sit down to make decisions, they often lack the common language, data, tools, experience, and signals needed to translate trustworthiness, as reflected in the OECD AI Principles, into something they can evaluate and act on.

summaryLinesEn: It works through four dimensions, (1) assessing risks and limiting what an agent may do up front; (2) keeping humans meaningfully accountable; (3) putting technical controls in place; and (4) enabling end-user responsibility.

To help answer these questions, a new Working Group on Agentic AI in Government, has been established at the OECD under the Working Party of Senior Digital Government Officials (E-Leaders) with a goal to seek to understand what governing with agentic AI should look like in practice, building on the OECD’s existing work on the agentic AI landscape .

feed.desc: Goldman Sachs Sees Limited Evidence AI Spending Is Crowding Out Other Investment    Yahoo Finance
summaryLinesEn: Goldman Sachs analyst Jessica Rindels estimates that U.S. investment in artificial intelligence will reach almost $600 billion in 2026, "equivalent to nearly 2% of US GDP."

That issue is particularly relevant because a significant portion of AI spending is directed towards imported technology equipment, potentially limiting the amount of investment that translates directly into domestic economic activity.

feed.desc: US-China AI trade decoupling ‘manageable’ – but tech curbs a ‘wild card’: Citi    South China Morning Post

feed.desc: Supply Chain AI Deployed by 88%, Governed by 12%: IDC Finds Trust Is Real Barrier    techtimes.com
summaryLinesEn: The survey, which covered more than 2,000 supply chain leaders across nine global markets, found that only 12% of organizations have AI planning governance fully embedded in their operations — while 41% expect autonomous AI to become their core operating model within one to two years.

A new IDC study released Wednesday found that 88% of supply chain organizations have deployed AI but lack the governance infrastructure to oversee it responsibly — a gap made urgent by an approaching regulatory hard stop: the EU AI Act's full compliance obligations for high-risk AI systems take effect December 2, 2027, and most operators have barely started.

EU Act's December 2027 Deadline: Sixteen Months and Counting The EU AI Omnibus, which entered force July 27, 2026, extended compliance for standalone Annex III high-risk AI systems from the original August 2, 2026 date to December 2, 2027 — giving supply chain operators additional runway but not eliminating the obligation.

summaryLinesEn: The IDC InfoBrief, which surveyed more than 2,000 supply chain leaders across nine global markets, found that while AI adoption is nearly universal - only 2% of respondents report no AI-enabled capabilities, and just 12% consider themselves AI leaders.

summaryLinesEn: That projection points to $1 trillion of AI-related investment around the globe in 2026, including $581 billion in the US, writes Joseph Briggs, who co-leads the Global Economics team, in a report.
